medical.title: First successful human challenge model for dengue serotype 4 could speed vaccine and drug testing
medical.summary: Researchers at the University of Maryland School of Medicine (UMSOM) and the Institute of Human Virology (IHV) have developed the first successful human challenge model for dengue serotype 4, a major advance that could speed the development of new drugs and vaccines against a strain of the dengue virus that remains difficult to study.

medical.title: New protocol finds ways to relieve overcrowding at hospital emergency departments, study finds
medical.summary: According to the CDC, an average of 155 million visits to an emergency department occur in the United States every year. More than a million of those patients spend at least 24 hours at the ED. This has led to an epidemic of overcrowding.

medical.title: Flu shots: Timing for maximum protection
medical.summary: Every year, as flu season approaches, many of us start thinking about how to protect ourselves and our loved ones from getting sick.

medical.title: Newly identified kidney protein protects blood vessels, study finds
medical.summary: As people age, or as certain diseases progress, their blood vessels can grow stiffer and less resilient. These changes can bring an increased risk of cardiovascular disease and earlier death. One trigger for blood vessel stiffening is a higher-than-normal level of phosphate in the blood. While elevated blood phosphate (hyperphosphatemia) is not common in the general population, it is much more widespread in people with chronic kidney disease (CKD) because their kidneys lose their effectiveness at filtering out waste products.

medical.title: Testing gel and a titanium brush for cleaning dental implants
medical.summary: Angela De Lauretis investigated how gels and a titanium brush affect protein coatings on titanium surfaces and cells' ability to adhere after cleaning. Her Ph.D. work provides knowledge that can inform the further development of methods for cleaning dental implants. The experiments were conducted in the laboratory, and the effects in patients need further investigation.

medical.title: A new tool to predict T cell behavior and improve immunotherapies
medical.summary: T cells are the trained killers of the immune system and the driving force behind cancer immunotherapy. But the behavior of T cells is hard to predict: Some spring into action when prompted, while others become lethargic and aimless. This puzzling inconsistency is one of the main reasons immunotherapies don't work in most cancer patients.

medical.title: New Public Health Alerts report spotlights how pregnant women with measles and their babies fare
medical.summary: With the United States teetering on the brink of losing its measles elimination status and cases across the country skyrocketing, a Public Health Alerts report today describes 112 cases of measles confirmed during pregnancy this year and last, the vast majority of them in unvaccinated women.

medical.title: Why don't GLP‑1 obesity drugs work for everyone?
medical.summary: Medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain semaglutide—a GLP‑1 receptor agonist that helps regulate blood sugar, appetite and body weight—have become household names and important pillars in obesity management for the medical profession.

medical.title: Five things that shape body weight—by an obesity expert
medical.summary: What you eat when you're tired and hungry might come down to what's open on the way home and what you can afford. Both appetite and access to food shape decisions that can look, from the outside, like simple matters of choice.

medical.title: WHO says countries need to 'move from plans to delivery' on antimicrobial resistance
medical.summary: New survey data released today by the World Health Organization (WHO) show that most countries have developed plans to address antimicrobial resistance (AMR). But few have implemented or provided financing for those plans.

medical.title: Babies rarely see exaggerated facial expressions used in emotion research, study finds
medical.summary: A new paper in Communications Psychology calls into question the value of exaggerated facial expressions commonly used in research to study babies' emotional understanding. The study, led by University of Kansas researchers, shows that babies ages 6–17 months rarely encounter these expressions in everyday life—and rarely see full faces at all.

medical.title: Measles is no longer considered eliminated in the US and Mexico
medical.summary: The U.S. has lost its measles-free status, international health officials said Tuesday, as the highly contagious virus once relegated to medical textbooks has spread—largely among the unvaccinated—at the highest rate in more than 30 years.

medical.title: Review examines pain mechanisms and offers a framework for personalized treatment of endometriosis
medical.summary: A joint research team comprising professor Kyeong A So of the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology at Korea University Guro Hospital and professors Jae-Wook Jeong and Tae Hoon Kim of the University of Missouri School of Medicine has comprehensively examined how pain develops and persists in patients with endometriosis. The team proposed new research directions to translate these insights into personalized treatment. Their review article was selected as a featured article in the journal Endocrine Reviews, highlighting its scientific significance and clinical relevance.

medical.title: New pill combo approved for breast cancer that stops responding to hormone therapy
medical.summary: People with advanced breast cancer that has stopped responding to hormone therapy now have a new pill-based treatment option.

medical.title: Study finds that feeling ownership of a pain-relief object may help increase pain tolerance
medical.summary: Pain relief may come from more than medication. A study by the Department of Psychology at Lingnan University has found that simply feeling a sense of ownership over an object believed to relieve pain may help people cope better with pain, even when the object itself contains no active ingredients. These findings have been published in The Journal of Pain and provide a new direction for exploring a low-cost approach to supporting pain management in health care.

medical.title: AI may help spot early signs of lung cancer in the blood
medical.summary: In a blue-and-white van outside Asda last June, 68-year-old Eddie, a retired fishmonger from Fallowfield, near Manchester, received life-changing news.

medical.title: As use of AI scribes spreads, researchers propose a framework for preparing medical trainees
medical.summary: Ambient AI scribes, which passively capture clinical encounters and draft notes, are among the most rapidly adopted artificial intelligence (AI) applications in health care. In one integrated health care system, they documented more than 2.5 million clinical encounters in a single year.

medical.title: New tool enables early intervention for diabetic foot ulcers
medical.summary: Australian researchers and clinicians have developed an AI-powered thermal imaging tool to predict if diabetes-related foot ulcers are likely to heal, potentially reducing hospitalizations and amputations.

medical.title: Intermittent fasting offers no additional benefits over the Mediterranean diet for reducing liver fat
medical.summary: A study led by the University of Granada and the Public University of Navarra has determined that, in the context of intermittent fasting, the time of day when one eats matters less than the amount of weight lost when it comes to reducing liver fat. The clinical trial, published in the journal JHEP Reports, included 197 participants aged 30 to 60 who were overweight or obese and compared three types of time-restricted eating (early, late and self-selected windows) with a nutritional education program based on the Mediterranean diet.

medical.title: Shoulder injuries rare but slightly more common after COVID vaccines than flu shots, study finds
medical.summary: Shoulder injuries are rare after a COVID-19 vaccination, but they may occur more frequently than they do after a flu vaccination, according to a new, large-scale study published in JAMA Internal Medicine.

medical.title: Clues to unexplained recurrent miscarriage found via genome sequencing
medical.summary: For many couples who endure repeated miscarriages, the search for a cause comes up empty: The embryos or fetuses have the normal number and assortment of chromosomes, and any routine ultrasounds prior to loss reveal no structural abnormalities. The lack of answers can be devastating for couples trying to build their families.

medical.title: Researchers develop DentalGEN, an AI framework for automated dental crown restoration
medical.summary: A collaborative international research team led by the Faculty of Dentistry of the University of Hong Kong (HKU) has developed DentalGEN, a large-scale controllable generative artificial intelligence-plus (AI+) framework for automated dental crown restoration. Their study, published in npj Digital Medicine, represents an important advancement in digital prosthodontics, smart dental manufacturing and Industry 4.0 applications in dentistry.

medical.title: Melanoma protein patterns help predict immunotherapy response, survival
medical.summary: Protein patterns in melanoma tumors can predict how patients respond to immunotherapy and can be used to find promising biomarkers and drug targets, according to two new University of Pittsburgh studies.

medical.title: Younger generations appear to have a double advantage against dementia, researchers find
medical.summary: Anders Fjell is the lead author of a new study that was just published in the journal Nature Medicine titled "Generational gains in cognitive capacity and dementia incidence rates in Western countries." The study is based on an analysis of about 219,000 people who have been followed for up to nearly 30 years.

medical.title: Common forever chemicals linked to nearly double the rate of aggressive breast cancer
medical.summary: An NIH study found that women with high levels of two common “forever chemicals” had up to 93% higher rates of an aggressive form of breast cancer. The discovery raises concerns about the potential health effects of persistent chemicals found in everyday products.

science.title: Study uncovers molecular mechanism underlying lip-related floral organ curvature in slipper orchids
science.summary: A research team from the South China Botanical Garden (SCBG) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences has uncovered a molecular regulatory mechanism that contributes to the development of curved floral organs associated with the distinctive lips of orchids, offering new insights into the development and evolution of floral forms in orchids. The study was published in New Phytologist on Nov. 6.

science.title: International Men's Day: Young men are struggling—but not all men are struggling equally
science.summary: Much of the news coverage on young men recently has focused on social media, gambling and the online "manosphere." But some of the most consequential changes in young men's lives are happening in school and workplaces.

science.title: Newly identified cell wall mechanism may help staph resist a last-resort antibiotic
science.summary: Antimicrobial resistance represents one of the major challenges facing modern medicine. Especially worrying are bacteria that develop resistance to antibiotics that are the last available treatment options.

science.title: Large companies can still fall short on their climate commitments. Here's what must change
science.summary: International climate conferences like the COP31 climate summit, now in its second week, tend to focus on the role of individual countries.

science.title: BPS Digital AVATAR Challenge
science.summary: The NASA Space Biology Program within the Biological and Physical Sciences (BPS) Division investigates how living systems respond across the full spectrum of biological organization to advance understanding of how living systems respond to the unique stressors of space exploration—including microgravity, ionizing radiation, low magnetic fields, and elevated CO₂. As NASA prepares for long-duration deep […]

science.title: New Album of Baby Star Sounds Shared by NASA’s Chandra
science.summary: A new album from NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory collects snapshots of baby stars across the galaxy and beyond and transforms that data into sound. Four new sonifications use data of stars that are actively forming, captured by Chandra and other NASA telescopes By studying places in the universe where stars are currently being born and […]

science.title: Records from 2,000 lakes reveal ecological changes moving increasingly in sync
science.summary: Although lakes cover less than 2% of Earth's surface, they play a key role in regulating global carbon, nutrient and biodiversity dynamics.

science.title: New research shows why human–AI collaboration requires more than task allocation
science.summary: A 2026 Strategic Management Journal study finds that successful generative AI collaboration in expert work depends on how organizations integrate fundamentally different forms of human and AI knowledge.

science.title: Unraveling bonding evolution in carbon-centered gold(I) clusters
science.summary: Gold nanoclusters, composed of a small number of gold atoms, can exhibit optical, electronic and catalytic properties distinct from those of bulk gold. One intriguing family consists of carbon-centered gold(I) clusters, in which a carbon atom is surrounded by several gold atoms. Unlike the familiar four-coordinate carbon in methane, the central carbon in these clusters can be coordinated by five or even six gold atoms.

science.title: Over a decade of atmospheric data from NASA's Curiosity rover hints at small amounts of surface water on Mars
science.summary: NASA's Curiosity rover has been collecting data about Mars' thin, carbon dioxide–rich atmosphere since 2012. Now, a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences has analyzed over a decade of this data to determine whether the daily and seasonal changes in Mars' atmosphere could be explained by known processes, including the freezing and release of carbon dioxide at its poles. What they found suggests a process involving water either attached to soil grains or in extremely thin, liquid-like films at the surface.

science.title: New nanoparticle MRI probe enables quantitative pH imaging
science.summary: The acidity of tissues can provide important clues about a disease. Tumors and inflamed tissues often become more acidic than their surroundings because of changes in cellular metabolism. Measuring these pH variations could help researchers understand disease progression, identify abnormal tissue environments and evaluate treatment responses. However, detecting small pH differences inside the body remains challenging because magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) signals are affected by the concentration of the imaging agent used.

science.title: Borneo forest survey reveals how mosquito abundance varies with river distance and height
science.summary: Several years ago, a researcher from Kyoto University was conducting fieldwork in Borneo in an effort to understand why certain primates frequently choose trees along rivers as sleeping sites. Among other potential hypotheses, he wondered whether there were fewer mosquitoes along riverbanks, allowing primates to sleep more comfortably. This question soon motivated him and his team of researchers to investigate how mosquito abundance varies between riverbanks and inland forests.

science.title: Quantum observers can 'agree to disagree,' but within limits, new theorem shows
science.summary: Two observers can start with the same description of a quantum system, follow the same probability rules and still disagree about the chance of the same outcome—even while being certain of each other's assessments.

science.title: Small life, big job: Enlisting microbes to fight climate change
science.summary: A working quarry isn't a pretty sight. Dust and bare rock, deep cuts into a hillside that appear like steps made for a giant. Nothing grows here, or so you would assume.

science.title: Liming soil could help protect crops during extreme heat waves
science.summary: New research has shown that liming soil to improve its pH buffering capacity could help plant roots survive heat waves and maintain crop productivity under high temperatures.

science.title: Building children's numeracy foundations involves more than 1, 2, 3
science.summary: As adults, we may take for granted what we know about numbers and how we arrived at this knowledge—for example, when comparing item prices to get the best deals or getting to appointments on time.

science.title: Pest mite overcomes catechin defenses in tea crops through a gene acquired from fungi
science.summary: Scientists have revealed how a major pest of tea crops can escape the tea plant's natural catechin defense mechanisms. The research, published in eLife provides convincing evidence that links an enzyme, DOG15, with the ability of a spider mite to adapt to and overcome the catechin-based defenses of tea.

science.summary: November 17, 2026 NASA’s NICER Telescope Ends Science Operations After studying the universe for six and a half years beyond its initial mission, NASA’s NICER (Neutron star Interior Composition Explorer) telescope on the International Space Station has ended science operations.  The mission and space station teams are now focused on plans to finalize NICER’s 8-year […]

science.title: Whom do we expect to put others ahead of themselves: Boys or girls? New study has surprising, and unsurprising, answers
science.summary: The holiday season is a time for gatherings with family and friends—as well as for less festive but necessary duties: organizing, preparing for and cleaning up after these gatherings. These are examples of service tasks that, according to previous research, women and girls are expected to perform.

science.title: Why punishment doesn't always prevent crime
science.summary: From "three-strikes" laws to longer prison sentences, harsher penalties are imposed in the hope they'll reduce crime. But decades of research show that increasing punishment often does surprisingly little. What if we're missing something crucial? New research from the University of California San Diego suggests one potentially overlooked reason: people's moral motivations for breaking the law in the first place.

science.title: Parting is sweet sorrow for parakeets—but a reunion might be worse
science.summary: Losing a member of the flock can create a ripple of disruption across parakeet society. But when a missing bird returns home after a prolonged absence, feathers will fly.

science.title: Meta-compass: An on-chip toolkit for visualizing optical spectrum and polarization
science.summary: A ruler turns length into a position on a scale. A thermometer converts temperature into the height of a liquid column. In each case, a physical quantity becomes easier to read because an instrument gives it a visible reference. We wanted to bring the same idea to light, whose properties are usually measured with separate optical components and then interpreted through additional data processing.

science.title: Available space reshapes cooperation and survival in new game theory model
science.summary: A theoretical study expands classic game-theory models of cooperation by allowing payoffs to change with available environmental capacity. Games such as the prisoner's dilemma help researchers explore how cooperation could have evolved in a world of limited resources.

environment.title: Rising preterm births in Bangladesh linked to extreme heat, research suggests
environment.summary: Hafsa Begum, 25, spent most of her recent pregnancy in a two-room apartment on the third floor of a five-storey building in a densely populated neighborhood of Dhaka, Bangladesh. Her bedroom remained dark even during the day, she says, as neighboring residential buildings blocked sunlight and restricted the flow of fresh air through the windows. […]

environment.title: Fossil of extinct giant bird discovered in Flores cave, Indonesia
environment.summary: Archaeologists excavating Liang Bua cave on the Indonesian island of Flores have identified a new species of extinct giant bird that roamed the region some 150,000 years ago, according to a recent study. The giant bird was a kind of megapode — large, chicken-like birds that today live in the broader Australasian region. These birds […]

environment.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

environment.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
environment.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

environment.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
environment.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

environment.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

environment.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

environment.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
environment.summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.

mix_items.summary: Statul român nu va mai avea atât de mulţi bani de subvenţii, scheme de sprijin şi vouchere pentru că resursele sale vor trebui direcționate către câteva domenii critice: apărare, educaţie, infrastructură, a transmis marţi consilierul prezidenţial Radu Burnete, antreprenorilor prezenţi la Topul Naţional al Firmelor Private din România. „Vă rog să fiţi realişti, şi pragmatici, …

mix_items.title: Un experiment științific în China a dus la moartea unei fetițe de 6 ani. Părinții au plătit 800.000 de dolari pentru finanțarea studiului
mix_items.summary: Un om de ştiinţă chinez care a ascuns moartea unei fetiţe de şase ani survenită în timpul unei experiment de editare genică, a fost demis în urma unei anchete realizată de autorităţile din Shanghai, potrivit presei de stat, informează AFP, preluată de Agerpres. mix_items.title: Când vor fi deschise pârtiile din Poiana Brașov. Reducerile pentru localnici în acest sezon
mix_items.summary: Tarifele pentru transportul pe cablu din Poiana Brașov vor fi menținute la același nivel ca în sezonul trecut, iar brașovenii vor beneficia în continuare de reducerea de 50% în fiecare zi de miercuri. Anunțul a fost făcut marți de viceprimarul municipiului Brașov, Dan Ghiță, care a precizat că pregătirile pentru deschiderea sezonului de schi sunt aproape de final.

mix_items.summary: Pe 21 noiembrie, Casa Tineretului din Timișoara găzduiește cea de-a treia ediție a conferinței I Choose You, organizată de Fundația Județeană pentru Tineret Timiș (FITT). mix_items.summary: Distincția, acordată în cadrul unei ceremonii desfășurate la Palatul Elisabeta din București, recunoaște contribuția inițiativei dezvoltate de Profi, brand din portofoliul Ahold Delhaize Romania, la promovarea tradițiilor, a micilor producători locali și a comunităților românești. mix_items.title: Trei eleve din Neamț au ajuns la spital, după ce au mers bete la școală și li s-a făcut rău. Ce amendă au primit părinții
mix_items.summary: Două fete în vârstă de 15 ani şi una de 16 ani, toate din judeţul Neamţ, au băut o sticlă de vodcă înainte de a merge la şcoală, iar când au ajuns la unitatea de învăţământ li s-a făcut rău şi au sunat la 112. Echipajele medicale le-au diagnosticat cu etilism acut şi le-au transportat la spital. Părinţii fetelor au primit câte o amendă de 500 de lei.

mix_items.summary: Fundația Motivation România se numără printre organizațiile care au contribuit la dezvoltarea Responsible Wheelchair Donation Toolkit, un ghid realizat de International Society of Wheelchair Professionals (ISWP), care promovează practici responsabile și sustenabile în donarea de scaune rulante, la nivel internațional. mix_items.summary: BMW Group introduce, începând din noiembrie, patru tipuri de propulsie pentru noile BMW Seria 7 și BMW X5: electrică, plug-in hybrid, benzină și diesel. Cele două modele integrează tehnologii...

mix_items.summary: BEST ELECTRIC VAN 2026: Ford Transit Curier, KIA PV5 Cargo și Iveco Daily au câștigat titlurile la cele trei clase, după două zile de teste. BEST ELECTRIC PICKUP 2026 este : Toyota Hilux BEV...

mix_items.summary: Ghid antibullying cu activități testate de mii de copii și 43 de ONG-uri. Articolul “Școala în care ne simțim bine” apare prima dată în World Vision România .

mix_items.title: Cursuri pentru tați și educație pentru sănătate orală în grădinițe: noi activități în programul “Start în educație”
mix_items.summary: “Start în educație” în anul școlar 2026-2027: 5 milioane de euro pentru îmbunătățirea accesului la educație timpurie de calitate pentru... mix_items.title: First successful human challenge model for dengue serotype 4 could speed vaccine and drug testing
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Maryland School of Medicine (UMSOM) and the Institute of Human Virology (IHV) have developed the first successful human challenge model for dengue serotype 4, a major advance that could speed the development of new drugs and vaccines against a strain of the dengue virus that remains difficult to study.

mix_items.title: REI Grup investește peste 2,5 milioane de euro într-o fabrică de ambalaje din hârtie la Călan
mix_items.summary: REI Grup, specializat în consultanță pentru atragerea de fonduri nerambursabile, a început construcția primei sale fabrici de ambalaje din hârtie kraft, la Călan, în județul Hunedoara. Investiția...

mix_items.title: New protocol finds ways to relieve overcrowding at hospital emergency departments, study finds
mix_items.summary: According to the CDC, an average of 155 million visits to an emergency department occur in the United States every year. More than a million of those patients spend at least 24 hours at the ED. This has led to an epidemic of overcrowding.

mix_items.title: De la timiditate la încredere: povestea unui tânăr care îndrăznește să viseze
mix_items.summary: Descoperă povestea lui Darius și cum sprijinul educațional oferit de Fundația Inocenți l-a ajutat să capete încredere în sine și să își urmeze visurile. The post De la timiditate la încredere: povestea unui tânăr care îndrăznește să viseze appeared first on Fundația Inocenți .

mix_items.title: Study uncovers molecular mechanism underlying lip-related floral organ curvature in slipper orchids
mix_items.summary: A research team from the South China Botanical Garden (SCBG) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences has uncovered a molecular regulatory mechanism that contributes to the development of curved floral organs associated with the distinctive lips of orchids, offering new insights into the development and evolution of floral forms in orchids. The study was published in New Phytologist on Nov. 6.

mix_items.title: International Men's Day: Young men are struggling—but not all men are struggling equally
mix_items.summary: Much of the news coverage on young men recently has focused on social media, gambling and the online "manosphere." But some of the most consequential changes in young men's lives are happening in school and workplaces.

mix_items.title: Flu shots: Timing for maximum protection
mix_items.summary: Every year, as flu season approaches, many of us start thinking about how to protect ourselves and our loved ones from getting sick.

mix_items.title: Newly identified cell wall mechanism may help staph resist a last-resort antibiotic
mix_items.summary: Antimicrobial resistance represents one of the major challenges facing modern medicine. Especially worrying are bacteria that develop resistance to antibiotics that are the last available treatment options.

mix_items.title: Newly identified kidney protein protects blood vessels, study finds
mix_items.summary: As people age, or as certain diseases progress, their blood vessels can grow stiffer and less resilient. These changes can bring an increased risk of cardiovascular disease and earlier death. One trigger for blood vessel stiffening is a higher-than-normal level of phosphate in the blood. While elevated blood phosphate (hyperphosphatemia) is not common in the general population, it is much more widespread in people with chronic kidney disease (CKD) because their kidneys lose their effectiveness at filtering out waste products.

mix_items.title: Large companies can still fall short on their climate commitments. Here's what must change
mix_items.summary: International climate conferences like the COP31 climate summit, now in its second week, tend to focus on the role of individual countries.

mix_items.title: Testing gel and a titanium brush for cleaning dental implants
mix_items.summary: Angela De Lauretis investigated how gels and a titanium brush affect protein coatings on titanium surfaces and cells' ability to adhere after cleaning. Her Ph.D. work provides knowledge that can inform the further development of methods for cleaning dental implants. The experiments were conducted in the laboratory, and the effects in patients need further investigation.

mix_items.title: BPS Digital AVATAR Challenge
mix_items.summary: The NASA Space Biology Program within the Biological and Physical Sciences (BPS) Division investigates how living systems respond across the full spectrum of biological organization to advance understanding of how living systems respond to the unique stressors of space exploration—including microgravity, ionizing radiation, low magnetic fields, and elevated CO₂. As NASA prepares for long-duration deep […]

mix_items.title: New Album of Baby Star Sounds Shared by NASA’s Chandra
mix_items.summary: A new album from NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory collects snapshots of baby stars across the galaxy and beyond and transforms that data into sound. Four new sonifications use data of stars that are actively forming, captured by Chandra and other NASA telescopes By studying places in the universe where stars are currently being born and […]

mix_items.title: Records from 2,000 lakes reveal ecological changes moving increasingly in sync
mix_items.summary: Although lakes cover less than 2% of Earth's surface, they play a key role in regulating global carbon, nutrient and biodiversity dynamics.

mix_items.title: New research shows why human–AI collaboration requires more than task allocation
mix_items.summary: A 2026 Strategic Management Journal study finds that successful generative AI collaboration in expert work depends on how organizations integrate fundamentally different forms of human and AI knowledge.

mix_items.title: A new tool to predict T cell behavior and improve immunotherapies
mix_items.summary: T cells are the trained killers of the immune system and the driving force behind cancer immunotherapy. But the behavior of T cells is hard to predict: Some spring into action when prompted, while others become lethargic and aimless. This puzzling inconsistency is one of the main reasons immunotherapies don't work in most cancer patients.

mix_items.title: New Public Health Alerts report spotlights how pregnant women with measles and their babies fare
mix_items.summary: With the United States teetering on the brink of losing its measles elimination status and cases across the country skyrocketing, a Public Health Alerts report today describes 112 cases of measles confirmed during pregnancy this year and last, the vast majority of them in unvaccinated women.

mix_items.title: Unraveling bonding evolution in carbon-centered gold(I) clusters
mix_items.summary: Gold nanoclusters, composed of a small number of gold atoms, can exhibit optical, electronic and catalytic properties distinct from those of bulk gold. One intriguing family consists of carbon-centered gold(I) clusters, in which a carbon atom is surrounded by several gold atoms. Unlike the familiar four-coordinate carbon in methane, the central carbon in these clusters can be coordinated by five or even six gold atoms.

mix_items.title: Why don't GLP‑1 obesity drugs work for everyone?
mix_items.summary: Medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain semaglutide—a GLP‑1 receptor agonist that helps regulate blood sugar, appetite and body weight—have become household names and important pillars in obesity management for the medical profession.

mix_items.title: Over a decade of atmospheric data from NASA's Curiosity rover hints at small amounts of surface water on Mars
mix_items.summary: NASA's Curiosity rover has been collecting data about Mars' thin, carbon dioxide–rich atmosphere since 2012. Now, a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences has analyzed over a decade of this data to determine whether the daily and seasonal changes in Mars' atmosphere could be explained by known processes, including the freezing and release of carbon dioxide at its poles. What they found suggests a process involving water either attached to soil grains or in extremely thin, liquid-like films at the surface.

mix_items.title: New nanoparticle MRI probe enables quantitative pH imaging
mix_items.summary: The acidity of tissues can provide important clues about a disease. Tumors and inflamed tissues often become more acidic than their surroundings because of changes in cellular metabolism. Measuring these pH variations could help researchers understand disease progression, identify abnormal tissue environments and evaluate treatment responses. However, detecting small pH differences inside the body remains challenging because magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) signals are affected by the concentration of the imaging agent used.

mix_items.title: Borneo forest survey reveals how mosquito abundance varies with river distance and height
mix_items.summary: Several years ago, a researcher from Kyoto University was conducting fieldwork in Borneo in an effort to understand why certain primates frequently choose trees along rivers as sleeping sites. Among other potential hypotheses, he wondered whether there were fewer mosquitoes along riverbanks, allowing primates to sleep more comfortably. This question soon motivated him and his team of researchers to investigate how mosquito abundance varies between riverbanks and inland forests.

mix_items.title: Five things that shape body weight—by an obesity expert
mix_items.summary: What you eat when you're tired and hungry might come down to what's open on the way home and what you can afford. Both appetite and access to food shape decisions that can look, from the outside, like simple matters of choice.

mix_items.title: Quantum observers can 'agree to disagree,' but within limits, new theorem shows
mix_items.summary: Two observers can start with the same description of a quantum system, follow the same probability rules and still disagree about the chance of the same outcome—even while being certain of each other's assessments.

mix_items.title: WHO says countries need to 'move from plans to delivery' on antimicrobial resistance
mix_items.summary: New survey data released today by the World Health Organization (WHO) show that most countries have developed plans to address antimicrobial resistance (AMR). But few have implemented or provided financing for those plans.

mix_items.title: Small life, big job: Enlisting microbes to fight climate change
mix_items.summary: A working quarry isn't a pretty sight. Dust and bare rock, deep cuts into a hillside that appear like steps made for a giant. Nothing grows here, or so you would assume.

mix_items.title: Babies rarely see exaggerated facial expressions used in emotion research, study finds
mix_items.summary: A new paper in Communications Psychology calls into question the value of exaggerated facial expressions commonly used in research to study babies' emotional understanding. The study, led by University of Kansas researchers, shows that babies ages 6–17 months rarely encounter these expressions in everyday life—and rarely see full faces at all.

mix_items.title: Liming soil could help protect crops during extreme heat waves
mix_items.summary: New research has shown that liming soil to improve its pH buffering capacity could help plant roots survive heat waves and maintain crop productivity under high temperatures.

mix_items.title: Measles is no longer considered eliminated in the US and Mexico
mix_items.summary: The U.S. has lost its measles-free status, international health officials said Tuesday, as the highly contagious virus once relegated to medical textbooks has spread—largely among the unvaccinated—at the highest rate in more than 30 years.

mix_items.title: Building children's numeracy foundations involves more than 1, 2, 3
mix_items.summary: As adults, we may take for granted what we know about numbers and how we arrived at this knowledge—for example, when comparing item prices to get the best deals or getting to appointments on time.

mix_items.title: Review examines pain mechanisms and offers a framework for personalized treatment of endometriosis
mix_items.summary: A joint research team comprising professor Kyeong A So of the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology at Korea University Guro Hospital and professors Jae-Wook Jeong and Tae Hoon Kim of the University of Missouri School of Medicine has comprehensively examined how pain develops and persists in patients with endometriosis. The team proposed new research directions to translate these insights into personalized treatment. Their review article was selected as a featured article in the journal Endocrine Reviews, highlighting its scientific significance and clinical relevance.

mix_items.title: Pest mite overcomes catechin defenses in tea crops through a gene acquired from fungi
mix_items.summary: Scientists have revealed how a major pest of tea crops can escape the tea plant's natural catechin defense mechanisms. The research, published in eLife provides convincing evidence that links an enzyme, DOG15, with the ability of a spider mite to adapt to and overcome the catechin-based defenses of tea.

mix_items.title: New pill combo approved for breast cancer that stops responding to hormone therapy
mix_items.summary: People with advanced breast cancer that has stopped responding to hormone therapy now have a new pill-based treatment option.

mix_items.summary: November 17, 2026 NASA’s NICER Telescope Ends Science Operations After studying the universe for six and a half years beyond its initial mission, NASA’s NICER (Neutron star Interior Composition Explorer) telescope on the International Space Station has ended science operations.  The mission and space station teams are now focused on plans to finalize NICER’s 8-year […]

mix_items.title: Whom do we expect to put others ahead of themselves: Boys or girls? New study has surprising, and unsurprising, answers
mix_items.summary: The holiday season is a time for gatherings with family and friends—as well as for less festive but necessary duties: organizing, preparing for and cleaning up after these gatherings. These are examples of service tasks that, according to previous research, women and girls are expected to perform.

mix_items.title: Study finds that feeling ownership of a pain-relief object may help increase pain tolerance
mix_items.summary: Pain relief may come from more than medication. A study by the Department of Psychology at Lingnan University has found that simply feeling a sense of ownership over an object believed to relieve pain may help people cope better with pain, even when the object itself contains no active ingredients. These findings have been published in The Journal of Pain and provide a new direction for exploring a low-cost approach to supporting pain management in health care.

mix_items.title: Why punishment doesn't always prevent crime
mix_items.summary: From "three-strikes" laws to longer prison sentences, harsher penalties are imposed in the hope they'll reduce crime. But decades of research show that increasing punishment often does surprisingly little. What if we're missing something crucial? New research from the University of California San Diego suggests one potentially overlooked reason: people's moral motivations for breaking the law in the first place.

mix_items.title: AI may help spot early signs of lung cancer in the blood
mix_items.summary: In a blue-and-white van outside Asda last June, 68-year-old Eddie, a retired fishmonger from Fallowfield, near Manchester, received life-changing news.

mix_items.title: Parting is sweet sorrow for parakeets—but a reunion might be worse
mix_items.summary: Losing a member of the flock can create a ripple of disruption across parakeet society. But when a missing bird returns home after a prolonged absence, feathers will fly.

mix_items.title: Meta-compass: An on-chip toolkit for visualizing optical spectrum and polarization
mix_items.summary: A ruler turns length into a position on a scale. A thermometer converts temperature into the height of a liquid column. In each case, a physical quantity becomes easier to read because an instrument gives it a visible reference. We wanted to bring the same idea to light, whose properties are usually measured with separate optical components and then interpreted through additional data processing.

mix_items.title: Available space reshapes cooperation and survival in new game theory model
mix_items.summary: A theoretical study expands classic game-theory models of cooperation by allowing payoffs to change with available environmental capacity. Games such as the prisoner's dilemma help researchers explore how cooperation could have evolved in a world of limited resources.

mix_items.title: As use of AI scribes spreads, researchers propose a framework for preparing medical trainees
mix_items.summary: Ambient AI scribes, which passively capture clinical encounters and draft notes, are among the most rapidly adopted artificial intelligence (AI) applications in health care. In one integrated health care system, they documented more than 2.5 million clinical encounters in a single year.

mix_items.title: New tool enables early intervention for diabetic foot ulcers
mix_items.summary: Australian researchers and clinicians have developed an AI-powered thermal imaging tool to predict if diabetes-related foot ulcers are likely to heal, potentially reducing hospitalizations and amputations.

mix_items.title: Intermittent fasting offers no additional benefits over the Mediterranean diet for reducing liver fat
mix_items.summary: A study led by the University of Granada and the Public University of Navarra has determined that, in the context of intermittent fasting, the time of day when one eats matters less than the amount of weight lost when it comes to reducing liver fat. The clinical trial, published in the journal JHEP Reports, included 197 participants aged 30 to 60 who were overweight or obese and compared three types of time-restricted eating (early, late and self-selected windows) with a nutritional education program based on the Mediterranean diet.

mix_items.title: Shoulder injuries rare but slightly more common after COVID vaccines than flu shots, study finds
mix_items.summary: Shoulder injuries are rare after a COVID-19 vaccination, but they may occur more frequently than they do after a flu vaccination, according to a new, large-scale study published in JAMA Internal Medicine.

mix_items.title: Clues to unexplained recurrent miscarriage found via genome sequencing
mix_items.summary: For many couples who endure repeated miscarriages, the search for a cause comes up empty: The embryos or fetuses have the normal number and assortment of chromosomes, and any routine ultrasounds prior to loss reveal no structural abnormalities. The lack of answers can be devastating for couples trying to build their families.

mix_items.title: Researchers develop DentalGEN, an AI framework for automated dental crown restoration
mix_items.summary: A collaborative international research team led by the Faculty of Dentistry of the University of Hong Kong (HKU) has developed DentalGEN, a large-scale controllable generative artificial intelligence-plus (AI+) framework for automated dental crown restoration. Their study, published in npj Digital Medicine, represents an important advancement in digital prosthodontics, smart dental manufacturing and Industry 4.0 applications in dentistry.

mix_items.title: Melanoma protein patterns help predict immunotherapy response, survival
mix_items.summary: Protein patterns in melanoma tumors can predict how patients respond to immunotherapy and can be used to find promising biomarkers and drug targets, according to two new University of Pittsburgh studies.

mix_items.title: Younger generations appear to have a double advantage against dementia, researchers find
mix_items.summary: Anders Fjell is the lead author of a new study that was just published in the journal Nature Medicine titled "Generational gains in cognitive capacity and dementia incidence rates in Western countries." The study is based on an analysis of about 219,000 people who have been followed for up to nearly 30 years.

mix_items.summary: A Swedish compensation scheme designed to encourage coexistence between reindeer herders and carnivores is facing growing criticism from Indigenous Sámi communities. mix_items.title: Rising preterm births in Bangladesh linked to extreme heat, research suggests
mix_items.summary: Hafsa Begum, 25, spent most of her recent pregnancy in a two-room apartment on the third floor of a five-storey building in a densely populated neighborhood of Dhaka, Bangladesh. Her bedroom remained dark even during the day, she says, as neighboring residential buildings blocked sunlight and restricted the flow of fresh air through the windows. […]

mix_items.summary: Archaeologists excavating Liang Bua cave on the Indonesian island of Flores have identified a new species of extinct giant bird that roamed the region some 150,000 years ago, according to a recent study. mix_items.title: Common forever chemicals linked to nearly double the rate of aggressive breast cancer
mix_items.summary: An NIH study found that women with high levels of two common “forever chemicals” had up to 93% higher rates of an aggressive form of breast cancer. The discovery raises concerns about the potential health effects of persistent chemicals found in everyday products.

mix_items.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

mix_items.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
mix_items.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

mix_items.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
mix_items.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

mix_items.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

mix_items.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
mix_items.summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.
